newsitem.title: FRANCE: EMU may give more stable fx rates - Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: EMU may give more stable fx rates - Tietmeyer.

text.p: The launch of Europe's single currency may provide a more stable relationship with the dollar and the yen if monetary union is accompanied by structural reforms, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said in an interview published on Monday.
"I think there is a chance of having a more stable relationship with the dollar and the yen," he said in an interview with the International Herald Tribune.

"An internally stable euro could produce more of a counterbalance. If it is unstable, that could create political tensions and there will be a temptation to seek a scapegoat among central banks," he said.
But Europe must implement structural reforms to its labour market to bring down unemployment, which he described as "the crucial issue for the future of Europe".
Tietmeyer also said there was a need to clarify the role of the future European Central Bank (ECB).

The newspaper said Tietmeyer, when asked to comment on French calls for a stability council to act as a counterbalance to the ECB, had recalled comments made by former Bundesbank president Karl-Otto Poehl.
"I found that statement very interesting and I think it is necessary to clarify this issue," Tietmeyer said.

Poehl, who left the Bundesbank in 1991, told a conference in Paris last week that French calls for a political counterweight to the ECB were extremely worrying and that for Germany, a basic condition for accepting the single currency had been to have a central bank as independent as the Bundesbank.

Poehl, who was involved in early talks on monetary union, said the agreement at the time was that governments would make major decisisions on the exchange rate system, but leave the day-to-day management of currency rates to the central bank.
French officials have said the management of the euro's exchange rate is too important to leave to central bank governors alone.

Tietmeyer also repeated a call for strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty when Europe's leaders decide in early 1998 which countries qualify to join monetary union when it is launched in January 1999.
"...the treaty is the treaty, and if politicians stick to that, then we will have to select the countries in a restrictive way," he said.

"Today it is not just a question of reaching a ratio in which the (budget) deficit equals 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, but also of sustainability, of those nations that have a stability culture. The question of sustainability is the crucial one," he said.
